title: Sun salutation, plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body as temple. Your line was this is where you live. What small kind thing did you do for the building? Day one hundred and twenty-six.
screen: `THE BODY AS TEMPLE — THIS IS WHERE YOU LIVE.`

segments.voice: If you've ever taken a yoga class, you've probably done it. Arms up. Fold forward. Step back. Down, up, dog, forward, rise. The instructor calls it a sun salutation, the music is soft, and everyone is mostly worried about their hamstrings. Nobody mentions the sun. But the name is telling you something. It isn't called the stretch sequence. It's a salutation, a greeting, and it's addressed to someone. Yesterday you walked slowly through the temple of the body. Today you move it, and point it at the original flame from day one hundred and twenty-three. Today: sun salutation, plainly.
screen: `ARMS UP, FOLD, STEP BACK.` → `NOBODY MENTIONS THE SUN.` → `A GREETING, TO SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Surya namaskar. Surya is the sun, the god you can actually see, from day one hundred and twenty-three. Namaskar is a bow, from the same root as namaste, your very first word. So: a bow to the sun. In its common form it's a flowing loop of about twelve positions. Stand with palms together. Reach up. Fold forward. Step one leg back into a lunge. Come into a plank, lower down, lift the chest. Push back into a mountain shape, step forward, fold, reach up, and return to standing, palms together. Each movement goes with a breath, in as you open, out as you fold. People who practice it as devotion often add something the gym leaves out: one of the twelve names of the sun, said with each round. The first is Om Mitraya namah: a bow to Mitra, the friend. Now, plainly, the history. Honoring the sun goes back to the Vedic hymns. Bowing to the sun at dawn is old too. But the exact flowing sequence taught in classes around the world was shaped and made popular quite recently, in the early twentieth century, by a raja in western India who promoted it for health. Both things are true. It's an old devotion wearing a fairly new shape. And so it can be two things at once: exercise, and a bow. Some Hindus do it each morning, facing east, as both. What makes it a salutation is the direction you face, and who you have in mind.
screen: `SURYA + NAMASKAR: A BOW TO THE SUN.` · `ABOUT TWELVE POSITIONS, ONE BREATH EACH.` · `OM MITRAYA NAMAH: TO THE FRIEND.` · `OLD DEVOTION, FAIRLY NEW SHAPE.`

segments.voice: A gentle version, three rounds. Skip anything that hurts; you can do it seated, just moving your arms. Stand, or sit tall, facing east if you know where it is. Palms together at your chest. Breathe in, reach up. Breathe out, fold forward as far as is comfortable. Breathe in, lift halfway. Breathe out, fold. Breathe in, rise all the way up, arms high. Breathe out, palms back to the chest. That's one. Twice more, slowly. If you'd like, say the friend's name with each round. Then sit, and notice whatever warmth is there. The bell holds the time.
Surya namaskar. A bow to the sun: a flowing loop of positions, one breath each, done as exercise, as devotion, or both. Today's word.
Your line: bow to the sun. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, face the light for one round, even just arms up and palms together. Day one hundred and twenty-six.

howItsDone: Many Hindus practice surya namaskar in the morning, facing east, as both exercise and devotion, sometimes reciting one of the twelve names of the sun, such as Om Mitraya namah, with each round.

original.note: Sanskrit: sūrya, the sun, and namaskāra, a bow or salutation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a yoga warm-up.
what it means: a bow to the sun, a loop of positions with a breath each, which some Hindus practice as both exercise and devotion.

what a scholar hears: the modern twelve-position sequence was popularized in the 1920s by Bhawanrao Shriniwasrao Pant Pratinidhi, Raja of Aundh, drawing on older practices of solar worship and prostration; the twelve names begin with Mitra.

notes: Please check the history: the Raja of Aundh's role in popularizing the sequence (1920s) and the title/date of his book (often given as 1928, English edition 1938).
The twelve names (Mitra, Ravi, Surya, Bhanu, Khaga, Pushan, Hiranyagarbha, Marichi, Aditya, Savitr, Arka, Bhaskara) are summarized; only the first is said.
The practice is a simplified, gentle version (arms and forward fold only) with a safety note; confirm it's appropriate.
'Many Hindus do it every morning, facing east' is general; practice varies.
